tagline: acceptEdits auto-accepts edits — except writes that **grant code execution**, which it stops to **re-confirm**.
summary: In **acceptEdits** mode, ordinary file edits apply without asking. But some writes aren't really "just edits": writing a **shell startup file** or a **build-tool config** means code runs the **next time a shell opens or a build runs**. So acceptEdits carves out an exception — it **re-prompts before writes that grant execution**, even though it's auto-accepting everything else. The boundary isn't the file's size or location; it's whether the write **buys arbitrary code execution later**.

sections.heading: Not all edits are equal
body: Auto-accepting a change to a source file is **low-stakes**: the code runs only when you choose to run it. Auto-accepting a change to **`.zshenv`** is different — that file is **sourced by the next shell**, so the edit is effectively "run this on my behalf, soon, without me looking."
acceptEdits draws the line exactly there. Editing application code: **accepted silently**. Editing a file whose **mere presence causes execution**: **stop and ask**.

sections.heading: What trips the prompt
body: Two families trip it. **Shell startup files** — `.zshenv`, `.zlogin`, `.bash_login` and kin — run on the next shell. **Build-tool config files that grant code execution** — things like `.npmrc`, `.bazelrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, or a `.devcontainer/` setup — run on the next install, build, commit, or container start.
The unifying test is **deferred execution**: does writing this file hand future code a way to run **without another prompt**? If yes, acceptEdits re-confirms; the auto-accept doesn't cover it.

sections.heading: A safety boundary, not a bug
body: It can look like acceptEdits "broke" — you asked it not to prompt, and it prompted anyway. It's deliberate: the carve-out keeps an attacker (or an honest mistake) from turning **one auto-accepted edit** into **persistent code execution** on your machine.
Read the extra prompt as the mode doing its job: the **blast radius** of an execution-granting write is large enough that even acceptEdits wants you to look.

diagram.caption: acceptEdits routes every write through one question: **does this grant code execution later?** If yes, it re-prompts despite auto-accept.

nodes.label: acceptEdits wants to write a file
nodes.note: The mode is auto-accepting edits. A write is about to happen without a prompt — unless the next check says otherwise.

nodes.label: Does this write grant execution?
nodes.note: The real test: not size or path, but whether the file's **presence causes code to run later** — on the next shell, install, build, commit, or container.

nodes.label: Ordinary file → accepted
nodes.note: Source code, docs, data. The edit runs only when **you** choose to run it, so acceptEdits applies it **silently**.

nodes.label: Execution-granting config
nodes.note: A shell rc (`.zshenv`, `.bash_login`) or build config (`.npmrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.devcontainer/`). Writing it arms **deferred execution**.

nodes.label: Re-prompt for confirmation
nodes.note: Despite acceptEdits, Claude **stops and asks** — the carve-out for writes that buy code execution without a further prompt.

nodes.label: Write applied after approval
nodes.note: Only after you confirm does the execution-granting write land. The boundary held; you looked before it armed.

scenarios.title: An ordinary edit is **accepted silently**
scenarios.note: Source files run only when you run them, so acceptEdits applies the change with no prompt — exactly what the mode promises.

scenarios.title: A config write **re-prompts** despite acceptEdits
scenarios.note: Writing `.zshenv` or `.pre-commit-config.yaml` arms code that runs later, so the carve-out stops to confirm before it lands.

misconceptions.myth: acceptEdits means no more prompts, period.
misconceptions.reality: It auto-accepts ordinary edits but **re-prompts before writes that grant code execution** — shell startup files and build-tool configs.
misconceptions.why: "Accept edits" sounds absolute. The exception is invisible until you edit a file that happens to run itself later.

misconceptions.myth: The prompt is about file location or size — system paths, big diffs.
misconceptions.reality: It's about **deferred execution**: whether the file's presence causes code to run on the next shell, install, build, or commit. A tiny `.npmrc` trips it; a huge source file doesn't.
misconceptions.why: We're used to permission boundaries being about *where* a file is. Here it's about *what writing it sets in motion*.

misconceptions.reality: Build-tool configs that grant execution are covered too — `.npmrc`, `.bazelrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.devcontainer/` and similar — not just shell rc files.
misconceptions.why: Shell rc files are the obvious vector, so the build-time ones are easy to forget — but a pre-commit hook or devcontainer runs code just as readily.
